messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Varying slopes LGCP model?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Finn,

Sorry, I took a few days off and returning to this now. Thank you very much for the clarification! Now I understand the + sp_id part of the formula, and yes, my bit of code was therefore wrong.

I have attached here what I believe is the mathematical formulation of my model (apologies for any mistakes). I have also added what I understand as a JSDM because I think comparing both models helps with the understanding of what I'm trying to do, and what I'm not trying to do (but still thinking about). Hope this helps!

Cheers

Em sexta-feira, 26 de julho de 2024 às 14:09:19 UTC+2, Finn Lindgren escreveu:
> Hi,
> I'm on holiday with limited email time.
>
> If your predictor depends on species, that must be part of the point
> process domain.
> I would _strongly_ recommend formulating the model without reference
> to any particular software implementation _first_. Then it's easier to
> see how to implement it.
> Starting with the code easily leads to confusion, as the software
> cannot always detect errors of logic in the model design itself, that
> are easier to spot in the raw mathematical definition of the model.
>
> When modelling multiple species as a point process, if the intensity
> only depends on space, you're modelling the superpositioning of the
> species-specific point patterns.
> If you want to model the individual point patterns, then the species
> label is part of the observation model. So you cannot have an
> intensity as function of geometry only, if the predictor takes
> different values for different species.
> You _must_ have it as lambda(space, species). This intensity is
> defined with respect to "per area and species", and is the same thing
> as a separate intensity function for each species.
> This is what
> formula = geometry + sp_id ~ ...
> means.
>
> So your last sentence seems correct, yes, and the last code chunk is
> incorrect, as it lacks the geometry + sp_id part.
>
> I don't have time to follow the details of the rest of the email now, sorry...
>
> PS. strategy = "simplified.laplace" has no effect in new INLA
> packages, as the new computation mode doesn't use laplace
> approximation in that step.
>
> Finn
>
> On Fri, 26 Jul 2024 at 13:25, 'Gabrielle Koerich' via R-inla
> discussion group <r-inla-disc...@googlegroups.com> wrote:
> >
> > Hi,
> >
> > Having explored this further and read more about the models, I have a few follow-up questions, including what I have been trying to implement now.
> >
> > My understanding of the model that I was implementing (please correct me if I'm wrong):
> >
> > spde <- inla.spde2.pcmatern(mesh = mesh,
> > prior.range = c(130, 0.01),
> > prior.sigma = c(0.1, 0.01))
> >
> > fm <- geometry + sp_id ~ 0 +
> > speciesIntercept(sp_id, model = "iid") +
> > twi(1, weights = rasters$twi, model = "iid", group = sp_id, hyper=list(prec=list(initial=log(1/30^2), fixed=TRUE))) +
> > field(geometry, model = spde)
> >
> > mod <- lgcp(fm, occ, samplers = iceFree1km,
> > domain = list(geometry = mesh, sp_id = seq_len(N)),
> > options = list(control.compute =
> > list(waic = TRUE,
> > cpo = TRUE,
> > return.marginals.predictor = TRUE),
> > control.inla = list(strategy = "simplified.laplace", int.strategy = 'eb'),
> > verbose = T, safe = T))
> >
> >
> > Is that the model is fitting different likelihoods for each species, while sharing the same spatial process for them. The model also fits species-specific intercepts and species-specific slopes by turning a random effect into a fixed effect (i.e. although where I get the output for the different slopes/coefficients is on summary.random I should interpret them as fixed effects). That means that I don't have a shared or a "population" intercept nor a shared / population coefficient for the covariate. My understanding is that I have single-species models bound together by a shared spatial effect, which is what + sp_id is doing in my formula. Is that correct?
> >
> > Now, I want to try to fit a model that has a shared group intercept / slopes (“population” intercept / slope) with species-specific intercepts / slopes (“clusters” intercepts / slopes), in the way that the model would be pooling information about them. I.e. the model would be estimating the population distribution of slopes at the same time that the model estimates each slope. So it would be “borrowing” information between species. I have come up with this solution (note that the spde is the same):
> >
> > fm <- geometry ~ Intercept(1) +
> > speciesIntercept(1, model = "iid", group = sp_id) +
> > twi(rasters$twi, model = "linear") +
> > twiR(1, weights = rasters$twi, model = "iid", group = sp_id, hyper=list(prec=list(initial=log(1/30^2), fixed=FALSE))) +
> > field(geometry, model = spde)
> >
> > mod <- lgcp(fm, occ, samplers = iceFree1km,
> > domain = list(geometry = mesh),
> > options = list(control.compute =
> > list(waic = TRUE,
> > cpo = TRUE,
> > return.marginals.predictor = TRUE),
> > control.inla = list(strategy = "simplified.laplace", int.strategy = 'eb'),
> > verbose = T, safe = T))
> >
> > So Intercept(1) would be the population intercept (fixed effect) and speciesIntercept the cluster intercepts (random effect). I then included the covariate as a fixed effect, and also as a random effect with species identifies, and set fixed to false to let the model estimate the precision. And I removed the +sp_id on the left side of the equation and from the domain in the model call, because then (in my understanding) it means that I'm fitting a single model for multiple species, while the different species / clusters coefficients are allowed to vary but still contribute and are influenced by the shared coefficients. And the spatial field is shared across all species.
> >
> > I want to confirm whether this approach is correct? And also understand better the use of the +sp_id on the left hand side of the equation. For example, if I'm interested in including a spatial field that is species specific, as you mentioned in one of the replies, as:
> >
> > spde_common <- inla.spde2.pcmatern(mesh = mesh,
> > prior.range = c(130, 0.01),
> > prior.sigma = c(0.1, 0.01))
> > spde_species <- inla.spde2.pcmatern(mesh = mesh,
> > prior.range = c(30, 0.01),
> > prior.sigma = c(0.01, 0.001),
> > constr = T)
> >
> > fm <- geometry ~ Intercept(1) +
> > speciesIntercept(1, model = "iid", group = sp_id) +
> > common_field(geometry, model = spde_common) +
> > species_field(geometry, model = spde_species, group = sp_id)
> >
> > My understanding is that then I would need to set +sp_id in the formula and in the domain, otherwise the model is not evaluating the spatial field by groups. Is that correct?
> >
> > Many thanks!

> >>> >>>>>> >>> For 2, one approach to build the model on the product space geometry +
> >>> >>>>>> >>> species, with something like
> >>> >>>>>> >>> domain=list(geometry=mesh, sp_id=seq_len(number_of_species))
> >>> >>>>>> >>> You didn't show enough of your code to see if you took that into
> >>> >>>>>> >>> account, but the iid2d model specification looks odd; the point
> >>> >>>>>> >>> process intensity needs to be a function of the domain coordinates.
> >>> >>>>>> >>> But it depends on what model you want to implement. E.g., if there's a
> >>> >>>>>> >>> common intensity, and you then model species _conditionally_ on the
> >>> >>>>>> >>> observed point pattern, then you can have a component that depends on
> >>> >>>>>> >>> sp_id,
> >>> >>>>>> >>> without having to include it in the point process domain.
> >>> >>>>>> >>>
> >>> >>>>>> >>> So the correct code depends on what model you're actually trying to
> >>> >>>>>> >>> implement; it's not clear what "this type of model" actually is!
> >>> >>>>>> >>> It's also essential to provide the like() calls you're using, as it's
> >>> >>>>>> >>> the combination of model components and predictor expressions&model
> >>> >>>>>> >>> families that define the model in the code.
> >>> >>>>>> >>>
> >>> >>>>>> >>> For 1, I don't see a problem with the code as written; to help debug,
> >>> >>>>>> >>> please run the model without the species component, to see if you
> >>> >>>>>> >>> still get an error; if you do, then there's a problem with how you've
> >>> >>>>>> >>> written the spatially varying coefficient definitions.
> >>> >>>>>> >>> Please run traceback() after the error to help identify what part of
> >>> >>>>>> >>> the code is throwing the error.
> >>> >>>>>> >>> For inlabru, the vignette to look at for spatially varying coefficient
> >>> >>>>>> >>> models is at https://inlabru-org.github.io/inlabru/articles/svc.html
> >>> >>>>>> >>> The INLA package version of the vignette isn't helpful for inlabru
> >>> >>>>>> >>> (and also hasn't been updated in a while).
> >>> >>>>>> >>>
> >>> >>>>>> >>> Finn

> >>> >>>>>> >>> >
> >>> >>>>>> >>> > I have been using a LGCP model for individual species distributions using inlabru. But I'm interested in now trying to fit a varying intercept and slopes model for all the species -- i.e. I want to get slopes for each covariate for each species.
> >>> >>>>>> >>> >
> >>> >>>>>> >>> > However, I am not sure how this would work in an LGCP model (or even if it's possible). I believe I was successful in implementing a random intercept model, but the part that is confusing me is the random slopes, especially because I have more than one covariate (7 in fact). So far, I have tried:
> >>> >>>>>> >>> >
> >>> >>>>>> >>> > How I coded the species:
> >>> >>>>>> >>> > occ$sp_id <- as.integer(as.factor(occ$scientific_name))
> >>> >>>>>> >>> > occ$sp_id1 <- as.integer(as.factor(occ$scientific_name))

Hi,
I will try to be concise, and please note that despite working with R for a while, coding for forecasting with Rinla is a whole new thing to me. I am trying to visualize the predicted number of infected cases following different forecasts. I would really appreciate any help on the below:
Using Rinla, I have selected the best model explaining the association between my outcome variable 'number of infected cases' and weather, socio-demographic variables....
The best model is:
SA3.ar_rw6 <- inla(ninf ~ 1 + f(Year,model="ar1") + f(Month,model="rw1") + IRSADdecile + lag1.meanTmin + lag3.meanDailyVariationT + lag4.meanDailyVariationT +
                     soi + lag2.soi + lag2.Rainavg + lag3.Rainavg + lag3.nino34sst + lag4.nino34sst + lag2.nino34sstanomalie +
                     lag4.nino34sstanomalie +  lag1.avghostseekingfemales +WC,
                   verbose = F,
                   data = data,
                   family = "nbinomial",
                   control.compute = list(dic=TRUE, waic=TRUE,cpo=TRUE),
                   control.predictor = list(link = 1))
summary(SA3.ar_rw6)

from this model, and after having collected and collated those forecasted variables under future climate change scenarios, I am having trouble with my results and am not sure I am using the right methods.

run model selected > extract posterior summaries

head(marginal_df1_6months)

ggplot(marginal_df1_6months, aes(x = MonthYear1, y = Mean1)) +
  geom_line(color = "blue") +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = Lower1, ymax = Upper1), alpha = 0.2, fill = "blue") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +
  labs(title = "Marginal Posterior Means and 95% Credible Intervals",

  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5, hjust = 1))+
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "4 years", date_labels = "%Y")

I obtain a plot with positive and negative values, which should not occur for a count variable.

2. predict_inla

# Ensure the model and prediction function can handle the extended timeframe
predicted_counts_historical <- predict_inla(
  model = SA3.ar_rw6,
  new_data = newdata,
  original_data = data
)
but this returns "  argument "df" is missing, with no default"
I tried to adapt the original function from github/gpw13/augury/R/predict_inla.R but in vain.

Any advice would be so welcome. Thank you.

then you can filter the output and only get predictions

mu = E * exp(eta)
size = 3
y = rnbinom(n, size=size, mu=mu)
r = inla(y ~ 1 + x, data = data.frame(y, x, E),
         family = "nbinomial", E=E,
         control.compute = list(config = TRUE),

         control.predictor = list(link = 1))

xx <- inla.posterior.sample(10^3, r, intern = TRUE)
sim.new <http://sim.new> <- function(E) {
    mu <- E * exp(Predictor)
    size <- exp(theta[1]) ## variant=0
    yy <- rnbinom(length(mu), size = size, mu = mu)
    return (yy)
}

yy <- inla.posterior.sample.eval(sim.new <http://sim.new>, xx, E = E)
plot(E*exp(eta), rowMeans(yy))

messages.body_plain:
I wanted to estimate the random effects using INLA. Here is the model using the frequentist approach

```
mod.freq <- glmer(cbind(n, N-n) ~ type + (1|subcounty) + (1|school_id), family = 'binomial', data = df)
```

I have tried to fit the same model in INLA using the formula:

```
formula <- n ~ 1 + type + f(subcounty, model = "iid") + f(subcounty, model = "iid")

mod.inla  <- inla(
  formula = formula,
  family = 'binomial',
  control.predictor=list(link = 1),
  Ntrials = N,
  data = df
)
```

However the results seem to differ especially in the overall intercept and in the random effects for both subcounty and Schoo_id. Additionally, when fitting the INLA model,I get a warning message:

```
*** warning *** iterative process seems to diverge, 'vb.correction' is aborted
*** Please (re-)consider your model, priors, confounding, etc.
```
Which is the best way to approach this. Thank you

messages.subject: Integrated species distribution models with presence-only and 'absence-only' datasets
messages.subject_clean: Integrated species distribution models with presence-only and 'absence-only' datasets
messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone,

I'm currently running a series of single-species integrated SDMs for twenty plant species in New Zealand. I have two datasets: presence-only data modeled as a Poisson distribution and presence-absence data modeled as a Binomial distribution. I am using the wrapper functions for INLA and inlabru in the PointedSDMs package to assist with building models from these data.

This method is working well for the species that have >20 presence records in both data sets. However, several of the species have plenty of presence-only records, but few (<20) or no presence records in the presence-absence data (presumably this is because these are all exotic species that have not become invasive enough in New Zealand to be present in the presence-absence vegetation plots). It seems that the literature on other formulations of presence-absence SDMs agrees that at least 20 records of species presence are required to make robust inference.

So, I have two questions:

(1) What is the best option for modeling distributions of species where there is presence-only data, and a data set with a presence-absence observation process that only contains records of species absence?
(2) Would inference from integrated SDMs constructed from presence-only and presence-absence data be robust if one of these data sets contained fewer than 20 presence records?

I'm leaning towards modeling these species with INLA as presence-only point process models with random spatial structure modeled as a Matern process with SPDE, but it does seem a shame to throw out information on over 40,000 locations where we know a species is absent. Keen to hear if there are any options for incorporating absence data.

Many thanks!
Sarah

messages.subject: CPUE standardization
messages.body_plain:
Hi all. I am trying to standardize a CPUE using INLA from a huge dataset (>90,000 observations) with 14% of zeros. I need to keep zeros, as they are important for the outcome. I am trying "tweedie" distribution and works fine for simpe models (only including year as response variable). But when adding variables to the model it chashes or takes hours to get any result (including errors).
This model works, although takes time:
f1 <- cpue ~ + f(year, model = "rw1")
I1 <- inla(f1,
           control.compute = list(dic = TRUE),
           family = "tweedie",
           data = data_FF)
But just adding month to the model, it is impossible to get something:
f2 <- cpue ~ + f(year, model = "rw1")+ f(month, cyclic=T,  model = "rw2")

I2 <- inla(f2,
           control.compute = list(dic = TRUE),
           family = "tweedie",verbose = T,
           data = data_FF)
And I was planning to add other variables that I consider to be important.
Any suggestion on how to improve the models? Any other distribution family that considers zeros in continuous variables?
Thank you very much.
Daniel

messages.subject: Mesh construction
messages.body_plain:
I'm trying to create a mesh over a specified region. However, inside the region, I have an area where data was not collected. Should I ignore the area and triangulate over the whole region, then remove the region after predicting? Below is the code which I am using to construct the mesh

```
nyeri <- county_shapefile |>
  filter(county == "Nyeri")
st_crs(nyeri) <- NA

outer_boundaries <- county_shapefile |>
  filter(county %in% c( all_hook$county)) |>
  st_union() |>
  st_sf()

kenya_shp1 <- as(as(st_transform(outer_boundaries, epsgKM(32737)), 'Spatial'), 'SpatialPolygonsDataFrame')
coords_mesh = coords.schs
kenya_shp <- fortify(kenya_shp1)
bdry <- inla.sp2segment(kenya_shp1)
shp.bnd <- cbind(kenya_shp$long, kenya_shp$lat)
c.bnd <- as.matrix(shp.bnd)

mesh <- inla.mesh.2d(
  boundary = bdry,
  loc = coords_mesh,
  loc.domain = c.bnd,
  max.edge = c(20, 40),
  cutoff = 1
)
par(mfrow = c(1,2))
plot(bdry);plot(mesh)

```

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Mesh construction
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
This really only matters if forcing the mesh triangle edges to conform to the inner region boundary makes the mesh needlessly complex.
What matters more is how you use the regions in the model; for point process models, you must specify the proper observation regions in the likelihood construction; this is separate from whether the mesh edges follow those regions or not.

Also, nowadays you shouldn’t need to convert to sp objects or sp2segment; the underlying fmesher functions accept sf polygons and do any potentially required conversions internally.

Finn

messages.subject: Seeking insight on model fitting
messages.body_plain:
Dear INLA Community,

I am seeking your insights regarding a model I am currently fitting: both a Generalized Additive Mixed Model (GAMM) and a Generalized Geo-Additive Mixed Model (GGAMM) using INLA.

In the process of conducting the GGAMM, I observed that spatial dependence was required; however, spatial independence was found to be insignificant. Notably, the inclusion of spatial effects improved model fitness, as assessed through DIC, WAIC, CPO, and AUC, and demonstrated superiority over the GAMM.

My question is: should I persist with the GGAMM, given its potential to capture unobserved variability at the micro level? If so, I would greatly appreciate any references or citations for further reading on this topic.

Thank you for your assistance.

Best regards,
Neamin

jp = function(theta, theta.desc = NULL) {
    ##for(i in seq_along(theta.desc)) print(paste0("    theta[", i, "]=", theta.desc[i]))
  p.mean <- theta[2*J+1]
  p.lprec <- theta[2*J+2]
  p.mean2 <- theta[2*J+3]

    lprior <- (sum(dnorm(theta[1:J], mean = p.mean, sd = sqrt(1/exp(p.lprec)), log = TRUE)) +
               dnorm(p.mean, mean = 1.5, sd = sqrt(1/exp(p.lprec)), log = TRUE) +
               (dgamma(exp(p.lprec), shape = 10, rate = 10, log=TRUE) + p.lprec) +
               ## to correct normalizing constants in 'generic'
               (-dnorm(0, sd = 1/sqrt(exp(p.mean)), log = TRUE)) +
               (-dnorm(0, sd = 1/sqrt(exp(p.lprec)), log = TRUE)))+
      (sum(dnorm(theta[(1+J):2*J], mean = p.mean2, sd = sqrt(1/exp(p.lprec2)), log = TRUE)) +

messages.subject: Bivariate model with inla.posterior.sample
messages.body_plain:
Dear INLA community

I am interested in simulate from the posterior of bivariate SPDE model to obtain the correlation between the two responses along the region. I have already fitted the model and obtained samples from the posterior but when I look at them I only obain values for one response.
For example, when one usually fit a model in INLA in this case to obtain the predictions for each we do:

idx.lead <- inla.stack.index(join.stack, 'Lead.pred')$data
meuse.grid$lead.pr <http://lead.pr> <- meuse.res$summary.fitted.values[idx.lead, "mean"]

idx.zinc <- inla.stack.index(join.stack, 'Zinc.pred')$data
meuse.grid$zinc.pr <http://zinc.pr> <- meuse.res$summary.fitted.values[idx.zinc, "mean"]

But here I am only able to get those values for one response, not for both of them, for example if my grid has 3000 points inla.posterior.sample.eval only get those 3000 points meaning that I have only one responde, not both of them. Is there any way to get both of them?

I add a code with an example I found in this paper and also add inla.posterior.sample.eval at the end to obtain the samples:

 Bayesian Inference for Multivariate Spatial Models with R-INLA by Francisco Palmí-Perales, Virgilio Gómez-Rubio, Roger S. Bivand, Michela Cameletti and Håvard Rue

https://arxiv.org/pdf/2212.10976

##############################################################################
############# Multivariate geostatistical analysis using R-INLA ##############
##############################################################################

# In this script, a multivariate geostatistical analysis of the concentrations
# of two heavy metals (Lead and Zinc) of the Meuse river dataset (available
# in the sp package) is performed using R-INLA.

# Load necessary packages
library(sp)
library(INLA)
library(maptools)
library(RColorBrewer)
library(gstat)
library(inlabru)
library(ggplot2)
library(rgeos)

# Load the data
data(meuse);
class(meuse)
str(meuse)

# Create the spatial object
coordinates(meuse) = ~x+y
proj4string(meuse) <- CRS("+init=epsg:28992")

##  Create the mesh for the INLA analysis

# Create a grid
data(meuse.grid)
coordinates(meuse.grid) <- ~x+y
proj4string(meuse.grid) <- CRS("+init=epsg:28992")
gridded(meuse.grid) <- TRUE
n.pred <- nrow(meuse.grid)

# Create the boundary
meuse.poly <- as(meuse.grid, "SpatialPolygons")
#Here a vector of 1s is used to put together all the little squares
ids <- rep(1, length(slot(meuse.poly, "polygons")))

meuse.bdy <- gUnaryUnion(meuse.poly)

# Extract coordinates of boundary
bdy <- meuse.bdy@polygons[[1]]@Polygons[[1]]@coords

# Create the mesh
mesh<- inla.mesh.2d(
  boundary = meuse.bdy,
  loc = coordinates(meuse),
  max.edge = c(250, 500),
  offset = c(250, 500),
  n=c(32, 32))

# Number of mesh nodes
nv <- mesh$n

# Create the spde model for the spatial effects
spde <- inla.spde2.pcmatern(
  mesh = mesh,
  prior.range = c(2394.16, 0.95), # P(practic.range < 2394.16) = 0.95
  # 4788.319 meters is aproximately the max distance
  prior.sigma = c(1000, 0.05)) # P(sigma > 1000) = 0.05
# An sd greater than 1000 would be a really
# high value, which is barely expected.

# NOTE: If you want default priors, comment the above lines and
# uncomment the following ones.
# #Create spde with default prior values
# spde <- inla.spde2.matern(mesh = mesh, alpha=2, constr = TRUE)

######## Build stack object

# Create the projector matrix
A.m <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh= mesh, loc = coordinates(meuse))

# Create the stack object for the cadmium
stk.lead <- inla.stack(
  data = list(log.y = cbind(log(meuse$lead), NA)),
  A = list(A.m, 1),
  effects = list(
    spatial.field.lead = 1:spde$n.spde,
    data.frame(Intercept.lead = 1,
               dist.lead = meuse$dist)),
  tag = "Lead")

# Create the stack object for the zinc
stk.zinc <- inla.stack(
  data = list(log.y = cbind(NA, log(meuse$zinc))),
  A = list(A.m, A.m, 1),
  effects = list(
    spatial.field.zinc = 1:spde$n.spde,
    base.copy.zinc = 1:nv,
    data.frame(Intercept.zinc = 1,
               dist.zinc = meuse$dist)),
  tag = "Zinc")

# Create the projector matrix for the prediction
A.pr <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh= mesh, loc = coordinates(meuse.grid))

# Prepare the data for the prediction
y.pred <- matrix(NA, nrow = nrow(meuse.grid), ncol = 2)

# Build predicting stack for the cadmium
stk.lead.pr <http://stk.lead.pr> <- inla.stack(
  data = list(log.y = y.pred),
  A = list(A.pr, 1),
  effects = list(
    spatial.field.lead = 1:spde$n.spde,
    data.frame(Intercept.lead = 1,
               dist.lead = meuse.grid$dist)),
  tag = "Lead.pred")

# Build predicting stack for the zinc
stk.zinc.pr <http://stk.zinc.pr> <- inla.stack(
  data = list(log.y = y.pred),
  A = list(A.pr, A.pr, 1),
  effects = list(
    spatial.field.zinc = 1:spde$n.spde,
    base.copy.zinc = 1:nv,
    data.frame(Intercept.zinc = 1,
               dist.zinc = meuse.grid$dist)),
  tag = "Zinc.pred")

# Stack for the shared effect
stk.shared <- inla.stack(
  data = list(log.y = y.pred),
  A = list(A.pr),
  effects = list(spatial.field.lead = 1:spde$n.spde),
  tag = "Shared")

# Stack for the specific sp effect zinc
stk.zinc.spec <- inla.stack(
  data = list(log.y = y.pred),
  A = list(A.pr),
  effects = list(spatial.field.zinc = 1:spde$n.spde),
  tag = "Zinc.spec")

# Put all the stacks together
join.stack <- inla.stack(
  stk.lead, stk.zinc,
  stk.zinc.pr <http://stk.zinc.pr>, stk.lead.pr <http://stk.lead.pr>,
  stk.shared, stk.zinc.spec)

t1 <-Sys.time()
#Build the formula
form <- log.y ~ -1 + Intercept.lead + Intercept.zinc + #Intercept.3 + Intercept.4 +
  dist.lead + dist.zinc + #dist.3 + dist.4 +
  f(spatial.field.lead, model = spde) +
  f(spatial.field.zinc, model = spde) +
  f(base.copy.zinc, copy = "spatial.field.lead", fixed = TRUE)

# Fix Gaussian precision to zero
zero.prec <- list(hyper = list(prec = list(initial = 15, fixed = TRUE)))

#Estimation
meuse.res <- inla(
  formula=form, verbose = FALSE,
  data = inla.stack.data(join.stack, spde = spde),

messages.body_plain:
Hi,
The question&answer you’re replying to are now very old, so I won’t try to answer in that specific context, but nowadays I would specify models with the help of interpolating or smoothing mappers in inlabru. E.g. for rw1 model, by specifying what values the model should be explicitly defined for as knots in a piecewise linear spline from fm_mesh_1d(), which then leads to linear interpolation between those knots. This is similar to the _effect_ of using inla.group, but with interpolation instead of rounding, and with more precise control over the model definition.

(One _can_ also do the above in plain inla() with A-matrices and inla.stack(), but inlabru exists partly so the need for explaining such complex user-side code can be eliminated.)

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] triple interaction random effects
messages.body_plain:
If you know how this age-space-time interaction term is defined, you can do
this. INLA use a one-dimensional indexing, so you only need to define a mapping
from

(age,space,time) -> index

which is unique and invertible. usually, age=1...N.age, space=1...N.space,
time=1...N.time, then one mapping is

index = age + (space-1) * N.age + (time-1) * N.age * N.space

jp = function(theta, theta.desc = NULL) {
  ##for(i in seq_along(theta.desc)) print(paste0("    theta[", i, "]=", theta.desc[i]))

  p.mean <- theta[31]
  p.lprec <- theta[32]
  p.mean.p <- theta[33]
  p.lprec.p <- theta[34]

  lprior <- (sum(dnorm(theta[1:15], mean = p.mean, sd = sqrt(1/exp(p.lprec)), log = TRUE)) +

               dnorm(p.mean, mean = 1.5, sd = sqrt(1/exp(p.lprec)), log = TRUE) +
               (dgamma(exp(p.lprec), shape = 10, rate = 10, log=TRUE) + p.lprec) +
               ## to correct normalizing constants in 'generic'
               (-dnorm(0, sd = 1/sqrt(exp(p.mean)), log = TRUE)) +
               (-dnorm(0, sd = 1/sqrt(exp(p.lprec)), log = TRUE)))+

Dear Professor Lindgren

Sorry if I step into the thread.

Referring to your message mentioning that INLA "overrides" the `strategy` argument (indeed models run with different strategies in the R command do yield identical results, even when in theory they should not),

Il giorno venerdì 26 luglio 2024 alle 14:09:19 UTC+2 Finn Lindgren ha scritto:
> Hi,
> I'm on holiday with limited email time.
>
> If your predictor depends on species, that must be part of the point
> process domain.
> I would _strongly_ recommend formulating the model without reference
> to any particular software implementation _first_. Then it's easier to
> see how to implement it.
> Starting with the code easily leads to confusion, as the software
> cannot always detect errors of logic in the model design itself, that
> are easier to spot in the raw mathematical definition of the model.
>
> When modelling multiple species as a point process, if the intensity
> only depends on space, you're modelling the superpositioning of the
> species-specific point patterns.
> If you want to model the individual point patterns, then the species
> label is part of the observation model. So you cannot have an
> intensity as function of geometry only, if the predictor takes
> different values for different species.
> You _must_ have it as lambda(space, species). This intensity is
> defined with respect to "per area and species", and is the same thing
> as a separate intensity function for each species.
> This is what
> formula = geometry + sp_id ~ ...
> means.
>
> So your last sentence seems correct, yes, and the last code chunk is
> incorrect, as it lacks the geometry + sp_id part.
>
> I don't have time to follow the details of the rest of the email now, sorry...
>
> PS. strategy = "simplified.laplace" has no effect in new INLA
> packages, as the new computation mode doesn't use laplace
> approximation in that step.
>
> Finn
>
> On Fri, 26 Jul 2024 at 13:25, 'Gabrielle Koerich' via R-inla
> discussion group <r-inla-disc...@googlegroups.com> wrote:
> >
> > Hi,
> >
> > Having explored this further and read more about the models, I have a few follow-up questions, including what I have been trying to implement now.
> >
> > My understanding of the model that I was implementing (please correct me if I'm wrong):
> >
> > spde <- inla.spde2.pcmatern(mesh = mesh,
> > prior.range = c(130, 0.01),
> > prior.sigma = c(0.1, 0.01))
> >
> > fm <- geometry + sp_id ~ 0 +
> > speciesIntercept(sp_id, model = "iid") +
> > twi(1, weights = rasters$twi, model = "iid", group = sp_id, hyper=list(prec=list(initial=log(1/30^2), fixed=TRUE))) +
> > field(geometry, model = spde)
> >
> > mod <- lgcp(fm, occ, samplers = iceFree1km,
> > domain = list(geometry = mesh, sp_id = seq_len(N)),
> > options = list(control.compute =
> > list(waic = TRUE,
> > cpo = TRUE,
> > return.marginals.predictor = TRUE),
> > control.inla = list(strategy = "simplified.laplace", int.strategy = 'eb'),
> > verbose = T, safe = T))
> >
> >
> > Is that the model is fitting different likelihoods for each species, while sharing the same spatial process for them. The model also fits species-specific intercepts and species-specific slopes by turning a random effect into a fixed effect (i.e. although where I get the output for the different slopes/coefficients is on summary.random I should interpret them as fixed effects). That means that I don't have a shared or a "population" intercept nor a shared / population coefficient for the covariate. My understanding is that I have single-species models bound together by a shared spatial effect, which is what + sp_id is doing in my formula. Is that correct?
> >
> > Now, I want to try to fit a model that has a shared group intercept / slopes (“population” intercept / slope) with species-specific intercepts / slopes (“clusters” intercepts / slopes), in the way that the model would be pooling information about them. I.e. the model would be estimating the population distribution of slopes at the same time that the model estimates each slope. So it would be “borrowing” information between species. I have come up with this solution (note that the spde is the same):
> >
> > fm <- geometry ~ Intercept(1) +
> > speciesIntercept(1, model = "iid", group = sp_id) +
> > twi(rasters$twi, model = "linear") +
> > twiR(1, weights = rasters$twi, model = "iid", group = sp_id, hyper=list(prec=list(initial=log(1/30^2), fixed=FALSE))) +
> > field(geometry, model = spde)
> >
> > mod <- lgcp(fm, occ, samplers = iceFree1km,
> > domain = list(geometry = mesh),
> > options = list(control.compute =
> > list(waic = TRUE,
> > cpo = TRUE,
> > return.marginals.predictor = TRUE),
> > control.inla = list(strategy = "simplified.laplace", int.strategy = 'eb'),
> > verbose = T, safe = T))
> >
> > So Intercept(1) would be the population intercept (fixed effect) and speciesIntercept the cluster intercepts (random effect). I then included the covariate as a fixed effect, and also as a random effect with species identifies, and set fixed to false to let the model estimate the precision. And I removed the +sp_id on the left side of the equation and from the domain in the model call, because then (in my understanding) it means that I'm fitting a single model for multiple species, while the different species / clusters coefficients are allowed to vary but still contribute and are influenced by the shared coefficients. And the spatial field is shared across all species.
> >
> > I want to confirm whether this approach is correct? And also understand better the use of the +sp_id on the left hand side of the equation. For example, if I'm interested in including a spatial field that is species specific, as you mentioned in one of the replies, as:

> >>> >>>>>> If all you want is to have different linear covariate effects for each

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] triple interaction random effects
messages.body_plain:
you can check like this

N.age <- 3
N.space <- 4
N.time <- 5
for(time in 1:N.time) {
    for(space in 1:N.space) {
        for(age in 1:N.age) {
            idx = age + (space-1) * N.age + (time-1) * N.age * N.space
            cat("time=", time, "space=", space, "age=", age, "idx=", idx, "\n")
        }
    }
}

you can have same 'idx' observered several times, that is no problem.

if your 'age' is not 1:3, as above, you need to map your age, into 1:3

>

>
> On Tue, 2024-08-06 at 21:25 -0700, Sarah Herbert wrote:
> > Hello everyone,
> >
> > I'm currently running a series of single-species integrated SDMs for twenty
> > plant species in New Zealand. I have two datasets: presence-only data modeled
> > as a Poisson distribution and presence-absence data modeled as a Binomial
> > distribution. I am using the wrapper functions for INLA and inlabru in the
> > PointedSDMs package to assist with building models from these data.
> >
> > This method is working well for the species that have >20 presence records in
> > both data sets. However, several of the species have plenty of presence-only
> > records, but few (<20) or no presence records in the presence-absence data
> > (presumably this is because these are all exotic species that have not become
> > invasive enough in New Zealand to be present in the presence-absence
> > vegetation plots). It seems that the literature on other formulations of
> > presence-absence SDMs agrees that at least 20 records of species presence are
> > required to make robust inference.
> >
> > So, I have two questions:
> >
> > (1) What is the best option for modeling distributions of species where there
> > is presence-only data, and a data set with a presence-absence observation
> > process that only contains records of species absence?
> > (2) Would inference from integrated SDMs constructed from presence-only and
> > presence-absence data be robust if one of these data sets contained fewer than
> > 20 presence records?
> >
> > I'm leaning towards modeling these species with INLA as presence-only point
> > process models with random spatial structure modeled as a Matern process with
> > SPDE, but it does seem a shame to throw out information on over 40,000
> > locations where we know a species is absent. Keen to hear if there are any
> > options for incorporating absence data.
> >
> > Many thanks!
> > Sarah

# Model formula

# Fit model with INLA
mod.mode.chl <- inla(formula.chl,
                     data=inla.stack.data(stack.est.chl, spde=spde_chl),
                     family="gaussian",
                     control.predictor=list(A=inla.stack.A(stack.est.chl), compute=FALSE),
                     control.compute=list(cpo=FALSE),
                     keep=FALSE,
                     verbose=TRUE,
                     debug=TRUE,
                     safe=FALSE,
                     control.inla=list(reordering="metis"))

messages.body_plain:
I apologize for that. Here, I am attaching the complete code, which is now working.

To clarify my specific doubt regarding this code: I have a bivariate model, and I am interested in using inla.posterior.sample and inla.posterior.sample.eval to obtain simulations of the predictions from the posterior predictive distribution to compute the correlation between the two responses.

This is the model:

formula <- y ~ -1 + b0.pb + b0.hg + ind + mar +
  f(s.hg, model = spde) +
  f(s.pb, model = spde) +
  f(base.copy.pb, copy = "s.hg", fixed = TRUE)

  I am using inla.posterior.sample and inla.posterior.sample.eval, but I am unsure if this is the correct approach when dealing with more than one spatial effect—one for each response and a shared effect. Since I am interested in obtaining the correlation between the two responses using the simulated values, I need to account for the covariance structure between the two outcomes. Is this the right way to do that with a bivariate model? Or is there another method within INLA to obtain the correlation between the two responses?

fun2 <- function()
  return(
    b0.hg +
      ind * cov1_region +
      mar * cov2_region +
      Ap %*% s.hg +
      Ap %*% base.copy.pb
  )

n_samples <- 5

samples <- inla.posterior.sample(n_samples, res)

prediccion_posterior_2 <- inla.posterior.sample.eval(fun2, samples)

fun3 <- function()
  return(
    b0.pb +
      ind * cov1_region +
      mar * cov2_region +
      Ap %*% s.pb +
      Ap %*% base.copy.pb
  )

n_samples <- 5

samples <- inla.posterior.sample(n_samples, res)

prediccion_posterior_3 <- inla.posterior.sample.eval(fun3, samples)

Thank you

> > Dear INLA community
> >
> > I am interested in simulate from the posterior of bivariate SPDE model to

> > look at them I only obain values for one response.
> > For example, when one usually fit a model in INLA in this case to obtain the
> > predictions for each we do:
> >
> > idx.lead <- inla.stack.index(join.stack, 'Lead.pred')$data
> > meuse.grid$lead.pr <http://lead.pr> <- meuse.res$summary.fitted.values[idx.lead, "mean"]

> > idx.zinc <- inla.stack.index(join.stack, 'Zinc.pred')$data
> > meuse.grid$zinc.pr <http://zinc.pr> <- meuse.res$summary.fitted.values[idx.zinc, "mean"]
> >
> > But here I am only able to get those values for one response, not for both of
> > them, for example if my grid has 3000 points inla.posterior.sample.eval only
> > get those 3000 points meaning that I have only one responde, not both of them.
> > Is there any way to get both of them?
> >
> > I add a code with an example I found in this paper and also add
> > inla.posterior.sample.eval at the end to obtain the samples:
> >
> >  Bayesian Inference for Multivariate Spatial Models with R-INLA by Francisco
> > Palmí-Perales, Virgilio Gómez-Rubio, Roger S. Bivand, Michela Cameletti and
> > Håvard Rue
> >
> > https://arxiv.org/pdf/2212.10976
> >
> >
> > ##############################################################################
> > ############# Multivariate geostatistical analysis using R-INLA ##############
> > ##############################################################################
> >
> > # In this script, a multivariate geostatistical analysis of the concentrations
> > # of two heavy metals (Lead and Zinc) of the Meuse river dataset (available
> > # in the sp package) is performed using R-INLA.
> >
> > # Load necessary packages
> > library(sp)
> > library(INLA)
> > library(maptools)
> > library(RColorBrewer)
> > library(gstat)
> > library(inlabru)
> > library(ggplot2)
> > library(rgeos)
> >
> > # Load the data
> > data(meuse);
> > class(meuse)
> > str(meuse)
> >
> > # Create the spatial object
> > coordinates(meuse) = ~x+y
> > proj4string(meuse) <- CRS("+init=epsg:28992")
> >
> >
> > ##  Create the mesh for the INLA analysis
> >
> > # Create a grid
> > data(meuse.grid)
> > coordinates(meuse.grid) <- ~x+y
> > proj4string(meuse.grid) <- CRS("+init=epsg:28992")
> > gridded(meuse.grid) <- TRUE
> > n.pred <- nrow(meuse.grid)
> >
> > # Create the boundary
> > meuse.poly <- as(meuse.grid, "SpatialPolygons")
> > #Here a vector of 1s is used to put together all the little squares
> > ids <- rep(1, length(slot(meuse.poly, "polygons")))
> >
> > meuse.bdy <- gUnaryUnion(meuse.poly)
> >
> > # Extract coordinates of boundary
> > bdy <- meuse.bdy@polygons[[1]]@Polygons[[1]]@coords
> >
> > # Create the mesh
> > mesh<- inla.mesh.2d(
> >   boundary = meuse.bdy,
> >   loc = coordinates(meuse),
> >   max.edge = c(250, 500),
> >   offset = c(250, 500),
> >   n=c(32, 32))
> >
> > # Number of mesh nodes
> > nv <- mesh$n
> >
> >
> > # Create the spde model for the spatial effects
> > spde <- inla.spde2.pcmatern(
> >   mesh = mesh,
> >   prior.range = c(2394.16, 0.95), # P(practic.range < 2394.16) = 0.95
> >   # 4788.319 meters is aproximately the max distance
> >   prior.sigma = c(1000, 0.05)) # P(sigma > 1000) = 0.05
> > # An sd greater than 1000 would be a really
> > # high value, which is barely expected.
> >
> > # NOTE: If you want default priors, comment the above lines and
> > # uncomment the following ones.
> > # #Create spde with default prior values
> > # spde <- inla.spde2.matern(mesh = mesh, alpha=2, constr = TRUE)
> >
> > ######## Build stack object
> >
> > # Create the projector matrix
> > A.m <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh= mesh, loc = coordinates(meuse))
> >
> > # Create the stack object for the cadmium
> > stk.lead <- inla.stack(
> >   data = list(log.y = cbind(log(meuse$lead), NA)),
> >   A = list(A.m, 1),
> >   effects = list(
> >     spatial.field.lead = 1:spde$n.spde,
> >     data.frame(Intercept.lead = 1,
> >                dist.lead = meuse$dist)),
> >   tag = "Lead")
> >
> > # Create the stack object for the zinc
> > stk.zinc <- inla.stack(
> >   data = list(log.y = cbind(NA, log(meuse$zinc))),
> >   A = list(A.m, A.m, 1),
> >   effects = list(
> >     spatial.field.zinc = 1:spde$n.spde,
> >     base.copy.zinc = 1:nv,
> >     data.frame(Intercept.zinc = 1,
> >                dist.zinc = meuse$dist)),
> >   tag = "Zinc")
> >
> >
> > # Create the projector matrix for the prediction
> > A.pr <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh= mesh, loc = coordinates(meuse.grid))
> >
> > # Prepare the data for the prediction
> > y.pred <- matrix(NA, nrow = nrow(meuse.grid), ncol = 2)
> >
> > # Build predicting stack for the cadmium
> > stk.lead.pr <http://stk.lead.pr> <- inla.stack(
> >   data = list(log.y = y.pred),
> >   A = list(A.pr, 1),
> >   effects = list(
> >     spatial.field.lead = 1:spde$n.spde,
> >     data.frame(Intercept.lead = 1,
> >                dist.lead = meuse.grid$dist)),
> >   tag = "Lead.pred")
> >
> > # Build predicting stack for the zinc
> > stk.zinc.pr <http://stk.zinc.pr> <- inla.stack(
> >   data = list(log.y = y.pred),
> >   A = list(A.pr, A.pr, 1),
> >   effects = list(
> >     spatial.field.zinc = 1:spde$n.spde,
> >     base.copy.zinc = 1:nv,
> >     data.frame(Intercept.zinc = 1,
> >                dist.zinc = meuse.grid$dist)),
> >   tag = "Zinc.pred")
> >
> >
> > # Stack for the shared effect
> > stk.shared <- inla.stack(
> >   data = list(log.y = y.pred),
> >   A = list(A.pr),
> >   effects = list(spatial.field.lead = 1:spde$n.spde),
> >   tag = "Shared")
> >
> > # Stack for the specific sp effect zinc
> > stk.zinc.spec <- inla.stack(
> >   data = list(log.y = y.pred),
> >   A = list(A.pr),
> >   effects = list(spatial.field.zinc = 1:spde$n.spde),
> >   tag = "Zinc.spec")
> >
> >
> > # Put all the stacks together
> > join.stack <- inla.stack(
> >   stk.lead, stk.zinc,
> >   stk.zinc.pr <http://stk.zinc.pr>, stk.lead.pr <http://stk.lead.pr>,
> >   stk.shared, stk.zinc.spec)
> >
> >
> > t1 <-Sys.time()
> > #Build the formula
> > form <- log.y ~ -1 + Intercept.lead + Intercept.zinc + #Intercept.3 +
> > Intercept.4 +
> >   dist.lead + dist.zinc + #dist.3 + dist.4 +
> >   f(spatial.field.lead, model = spde) +
> >   f(spatial.field.zinc, model = spde) +
> >   f(base.copy.zinc, copy = "spatial.field.lead", fixed = TRUE)
> >
> > # Fix Gaussian precision to zero
> > zero.prec <- list(hyper = list(prec = list(initial = 15, fixed = TRUE)))
> >
> > #Estimation
> > meuse.res <- inla(
> >   formula=form, verbose = FALSE,
> >   data = inla.stack.data(join.stack, spde = spde),
> >   family = rep("gaussian", 2),
> >   control.family = list(zero.prec, zero.prec),
> >   control.predictor = list(A = inla.stack.A(join.stack),
> >                            compute = TRUE),
> >   control.compute = list(dic = TRUE, waic = TRUE,
> >                          cpo = TRUE, mlik = TRUE, po = TRUE,
> >                          config = TRUE))#
> >
> > summary(meuse.res)
> >
> >
> >
> > # Extract the estimates for plotting lead density
> > idx.lead <- inla.stack.index(join.stack, 'Lead.pred')$data
> > meuse.grid$lead.pr <http://lead.pr> <- meuse.res$summary.fitted.values[idx.lead, "mean"]
> >
> > # Extract the estimates for plotting zinc density
> > idx.zinc <- inla.stack.index(join.stack, 'Zinc.pred')$data
> > meuse.grid$zinc.pr <http://zinc.pr> <- meuse.res$summary.fitted.values[idx.zinc, "mean"]
> >
> > # Extract the post. mean of the shared effect
> > idx.shared <- inla.stack.index(join.stack, 'Shared')$data
> > meuse.grid$shared <- meuse.res$summary.fitted.values[idx.shared, "mean"]
> >
> > # Extract the post. mean of the zinc specific effect
> > idx.zinc.spec <- inla.stack.index(join.stack, 'Zinc.spec')$data
> > meuse.grid$zinc.spec <- meuse.res$summary.fitted.values[idx.zinc.spec, "mean"]
> >
> >
> > fun2 <- function()
> >   return(
> >     Intercept.lead + Intercept.zinc +
> >       dist.lead*meuse.grid$dist + dist.zinc*meuse.grid$dist +
> >       A.pr %*% spatial.field.lead +
> >       A.pr %*% spatial.field.zinc +
> >       A.pr %*% base.copy.zinc
> >
> >   )
> >
> > n_samples <- 5
> >
> > samples <- inla.posterior.sample(n_samples, meuse.res)
> >
> > prediccion_posterior_2 <- inla.posterior.sample.eval(fun2, samples)
> >
> >
> >
> > Here if I want to obtained the simulated values from prediccion_posterior_2 I
> > would do
> >
> > > prediccion_posterior_2[[1]]@x
> >
> > And I would get 3103 values that is the same number of points that meuse.grid
> > has but if we assume that is the obtained values of the first response and I

> >
> > Thank you!!

messages.body_plain:
Hello, I have two questions:

1. I used an empirical Variogram to estimate the value of the range, (the point where the variogram starts to level off) and also the variance (Total variance minus the nugget from the variogram) and used this values in the SPDE model

```
spde <- inla.spde2.pcmatern(
  mesh = mesh,
  alpha = 2,
  constr = TRUE,
  prior.range = c(200, .5),   # P(range < 200) = .5
  prior.sigma = c(0.23, .5)   # P(sigma > 0.23) = .5
)
```
What do you think about this?

2. When fitting the model itself, I get the warnings:

*** warning *** iterative process seems to diverge, 'vb.correction' is aborted
*** Please (re-)consider your model, priors, confounding, etc.
I have no missing values in my covariates. What could be causing this.

Here is the code I used for the model:

```
mod <- inla(
  formula,
  family = "binomial",
  Ntrials = numtrials,
  data = inla.stack.data(stk.full),
  control.family = control.family(link = 'logit'),
  control.predictor = list(
    compute = TRUE,
    link = 1,
    A = inla.stack.A(stk.full)
  ),
  control.compute = list(config = TRUE, return.marginals.predictor = TRUE),
  control.inla = list(tolerance = 1e-7),
  num.threads = 7,
  verbose = F
)
```

messages.subject: Different results between executions
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I am fitting the first two spatio-temporal models discussed in https://doi.org/10.1016/j.sste.2012.12.001which correspond to:

response ~ 1 +
f(ID.site , model="bym", graph = Hurricanes .adj) +
f(ID.site1 , year.vector , model = "iid") +
year.vector

and

response ~ 1 +
f(ID.site , model="bym", graph = Hurricanes .adj) +
f(ID.year , model = "rw1") +
f(ID.year1 , model = "iid")

For both models the results for the structured (besag) part of the BYM specification is consistent. For the first model the interaction is also consistent, and for the second model the iid part (indexed by time) is consistent too. However, between executions the unstructured (iid part) part of the BYM changes values for both models, sometimes drastically (from e-04 to e-05 in scale), as well as random walk of order 1 in the second model.

I am not sure whether this is due to numerical instabilities, or identifiability issues.
I have tried to insert more constraints such separating the BYM into a besag + iid and setting a sum to 0 constraint in the iid part, or adding a sum to zero constraint on the iid part (indexed by time), but it does not seem to work.

I also set a seed (set.seed(0)). Does anyone have any possible explanation for what is happening?

Thank you for your time and consideration,
Ismael Ahmad

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Different results between executions
messages.body_plain:
Sorry for how messy things are. I mean to state that I get consistency problems when executing a particular model various times, and that this occurs for both models. That is to say

SPASIBA.test02<-function (geno.ref, ploidy, coord.ref, sphere = FALSE, size.pop.ref,
                          geno.unknown, quant.ref = NULL, quant.unknown = NULL, make.inf = FALSE,
                          loc.infcov = NULL, kappa.geno.plug = NULL, tau.geno.plug = NULL,
                          window = NULL, max.edge.mesh = NULL, offset.mesh = -0.1,
                          marginal.quant = "none", make.pred = FALSE, nx.pred = 20,
                          ny.pred = 20, make.assign = FALSE, proj.predref = NULL,
                          freq.predref = NULL, verbose.inf = TRUE, verbose.pred = TRUE)
{
  lonlat3D = function(lon, lat) {
    cbind(cos((lon/180) * pi) * cos((lat/180) * pi), sin((lon/180) *
                                                           pi) * cos((lat/180) * pi), sin((lat/180) * pi))
  }
  if (!(marginal.quant %in% c("none", "norm", "lnorm")))
    stop("marginal.quant should be none, norm or lnorm")
  mesh.predref <- omesh.predref <- NULL
  use.quant <- !is.null(quant.ref)
  use.geno <- !is.null(geno.ref)
  final.res <- NULL
  true.radius.of.earth = 6371
  if (is.null(window)) {
    xmin <- min(coord.ref[, 1])
    xmax <- max(coord.ref[, 1])
    ymin <- min(coord.ref[, 2])
    ymax <- max(coord.ref[, 2])
  }
  else {
    xmin <- min(window[, 1])
    xmax <- max(window[, 1])
    ymin <- min(window[, 2])
    ymax <- max(window[, 2])
  }
  if (is.null(max.edge.mesh)) {
    max.edge.mesh = 0.1 * max(xmax - xmin, ymax - ymin)
  }
  if (use.geno) {
    n.loc <- ncol(geno.ref)
    if (is.null(loc.infcov)) {
      loc.infcov <- 1:n.loc
    }
    n.loc.infcov <- length(loc.infcov)
    n.unknown <- ifelse(is.null(geno.unknown), 0, nrow(geno.unknown))
  }
  if (use.quant) {
    n.quant <- ncol(quant.ref)
    n.unknown <- ifelse(is.null(quant.unknown), 0, nrow(quant.unknown))
  }
  if (use.geno) {
    if (!make.inf) {
      print("PLUGGING COVARIANCE PARAMETERS")
      kappa.geno.est <- kappa.geno.plug
      tau.geno.est <- tau.geno.plug
    }
    else {
      if (sphere) {
        coord.tmp <- lonlat3D(coord.ref[, 1], coord.ref[,
                                                        2])
        window <- lonlat3D(window[, 1], window[, 2])
      }
      else {
        coord.tmp <- coord.ref
      }
      print("")
      print("Estimating covariance parameters")
      mesh.ref <- inla.mesh.2d(loc = coord.tmp, loc.domain = window,
                               offset = offset.mesh, max.edge = max.edge.mesh,
                               cutoff = 0)
      spde.infcov = inla.spde.create(mesh.ref, model = "matern",
                                     param = list(alpha = 2))
      if (!sphere) {
        data.df <- data.frame(xcoord = rep(coord.tmp[,
                                                     1], n.loc.infcov), ycoord = rep(coord.tmp[,
                                                                                               2], n.loc.infcov), allele.counts = as.vector(geno.ref[,
                                                                                                                                                     loc.infcov]), size = as.vector(size.pop.ref[,
                                                                                                                                                                                                 loc.infcov]), spatial = rep(mesh.ref$idx$loc,
                                                                                                                                                                                                                             n.loc.infcov))
      }
      else {
        data.df <- data.frame(xcoord = rep(coord.tmp[,
                                                     1], n.loc.infcov), ycoord = rep(coord.tmp[,
                                                                                               2], n.loc.infcov), zcoord = rep(coord.tmp[,
                                                                                                                                         3], n.loc.infcov), allele.counts = as.vector(geno.ref[,
                                                                                                                                                                                               loc.infcov]), size = as.vector(size.pop.ref[,
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           loc.infcov]), spatial = rep(mesh.ref$idx$loc,
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       n.loc.infcov))
      }
      r = rep(1:n.loc.infcov, each = nrow(coord.ref))
      formula = (allele.counts ~ -1 + as.factor(r) + f(spatial,
                                                       model = spde.infcov, replicate = r))
      result.infcov <- (inla(formula, family = "binomial",
                             Ntrials = as.vector(size.pop.ref[, loc.infcov]),
                             data = data.df, control.family = list(link = "logit"), control.predictor=list(link= 1),
                             control.compute = list(openmp.strategy="huge", return.marginals = FALSE),
                             control.inla = list(tolerance = 1e-05), verbose = verbose.inf))
      tau.geno.est = exp(result.infcov$summary.hyperpar[1,
                                                        "mean"])
      kappa.geno.est = exp(result.infcov$summary.hyperpar[2,
                                                          "mean"]/2)
      final.res <- append(final.res, list(mesh.ref = mesh.ref,
                                          cpu.used.infcov = result.infcov$cpu.used, tau.geno.est = tau.geno.est,
                                          kappa.geno.est = kappa.geno.est, make.inf = make.inf))
    }
  }
  if (make.pred) {
    cpu.used.predfreq.perloc <- matrix(nrow = ncol(geno.ref),
                                       ncol = 4)
    print("")
    print("Mapping allele frequencies")
    n.pred <- nx.pred * ny.pred
    coord.pred <- matrix(nrow = n.pred, ncol = 2)
    coord.pred[, 1] <- rep(seq(xmin, xmax, l = nx.pred),
                           ny.pred)
    coord.pred[, 2] <- as.vector(matrix(nrow = nx.pred,
                                        ncol = ny.pred, byrow = TRUE, rep(seq(ymin, ymax,
                                                                              l = ny.pred), nx.pred)))
    final.res <- append(final.res, list(coord.pred = coord.pred))
    coord.predref <- rbind(coord.pred, coord.ref)
    if (!sphere) {
      coord.predref.tmp <- coord.predref
    }
    else {
      coord.predref.tmp <- lonlat3D(coord.predref[, 1],
                                    coord.predref[, 2])
      window <- lonlat3D(window[, 1], window[, 2])
    }
    print("Starting to creat mesh")
    mesh.predref <- inla.mesh.2d(loc = coord.predref.tmp,
                                 loc.domain = window, offset = offset.mesh, max.edge = max.edge.mesh,
                                 cutoff = 0)
    print("Mesh creating completed")
    if (use.geno) {
      size.pop.pred <- matrix(nrow = n.pred, ncol = n.loc,
                              2)
      y.pred <- matrix(nrow = n.pred, ncol = n.loc)
      y.predref <- rbind(y.pred, geno.ref)
      size.pop.predref <- rbind(size.pop.pred, size.pop.ref)
      spde.predref <- inla.spde2.matern(mesh.predref,
                                        B.tau = matrix(log(tau.geno.est), 1, 1), B.kappa = matrix(log(kappa.geno.est),
                                                                                                  1, 1))
      proj.predref <- inla.mesh.projector(mesh.predref,
                                          dims = c(nx.pred, ny.pred), xlim = c(xmin, xmax),
                                          ylim = c(ymin, ymax))
      u <- proj.predref$x
      v <- proj.predref$y
      formula = (allele.counts ~ 1 + f(spatial, model = spde.predref))
      for (iloc in 1:n.loc) {
        print(paste("locus ", iloc))
        if (!sphere) {
          data.df <- data.frame(xcoord = coord.predref.tmp[,
                                                           1], ycoord = coord.predref.tmp[, 2], allele.counts = y.predref[,
                                                                                                                          iloc], size = size.pop.predref[, iloc],
                                spatial = mesh.predref$idx$loc)
        }
        else {
          data.df <- data.frame(xcoord = coord.predref.tmp[,
                                                           1], ycoord = coord.predref.tmp[, 2], zcoord = coord.predref.tmp[,
                                                                                                                           3], allele.counts = y.predref[, iloc], size = size.pop.predref[,
                                                                                                                                                                                          iloc], spatial = mesh.predref$idx$loc)
        }
        result.predref <- (inla(formula, family = "binomial",
                                Ntrials = size.pop.predref[, iloc], data = data.df,
                                control.family = list(link = "logit"), control.compute = list(openmp.strategy="huge", return.marginals = FALSE), control.predictor=list(link= 1),
                                control.inla = list(tolerance = 1e-05), verbose = verbose.pred))
        cpu.used.predfreq.perloc[iloc, ] <- result.predref$cpu.used
        n.mesh.spde.predref <- length(result.predref$summary.random$spatial[,
                                                                            "mean"])
        if (iloc == 1) {
          tmp <- inla.mesh.project(proj.predref, result.predref$summary.random$spatial[,
                                                                                       "mean"])
          gf.geno.predref <- freq.predref <- array(dim = c(nrow(tmp),
                                                           ncol(tmp), n.loc))
          gf.geno.predref[, , 1] <- tmp
        }
        else {
          gf.geno.predref[, , iloc] <- inla.mesh.project(proj.predref,
                                                         result.predref$summary.random$spatial[,
                                                                                               "mean"])
        }
        freq.predref[, , iloc] <- 1/(1 + exp(-(as.numeric(result.predref$summary.fixed[1]) +
                                                 gf.geno.predref[, , iloc])))
      }
    }
    if (use.quant) {
      spde.predref <- inla.spde.create(mesh.predref, model = "matern",
                                       param = list(alpha = 2))
      proj.predref <- inla.mesh.projector(mesh.predref,
                                          dims = c(nx.pred, ny.pred), xlim = c(xmin, xmax),
                                          ylim = c(ymin, ymax))
      u <- proj.predref$x
      v <- proj.predref$y
      event <- rep(1, nrow(coord.predref.tmp))
      if (marginal.quant == "norm") {
        formula = (quant ~ 1 + f(spatial, model = spde.predref))
        family.quant <- "gaussian"
      }
      if (marginal.quant == "lnorm") {
        formula <- (inla.surv(quant, event) ~ 1 + f(spatial,
                                                    model = spde.predref))
        family.quant <- "lognormal"
      }
      mean.quant <- sd.noise.quant <- rep(NA, n.quant)
      for (iquant in 1:n.quant) {
        print(paste("quantitative variable ", iquant))
        if (!sphere) {
          data.df <- data.frame(xcoord = coord.predref.tmp[,
                                                           1], ycoord = coord.predref.tmp[, 2], quant = c(rep(NA,
                                                                                                              n.pred), quant.ref[, iquant]), event = event,
                                spatial = mesh.predref$idx$loc)
        }
        else {
          data.df <- data.frame(xcoord = coord.predref.tmp[,
                                                           1], ycoord = coord.predref.tmp[, 2], zcoord = coord.predref.tmp[,
                                                                                                                           3], quant = c(rep(NA, n.pred), quant.ref[,
                                                                                                                                                                    iquant]), event = event, spatial = mesh.predref$idx$loc)
        }
        result.predref <- (inla(formula, family = family.quant,
                                data = data.df, verbose = verbose.pred))
        mean.quant[iquant] <- result.predref$summary.fixed[,
                                                           "mean"]
        sd.noise.quant[iquant] <- inla.emarginal(function(x) sqrt(1/x),
                                                 result.predref$marginals.hyperpar[[1]])
        if (iquant == 1) {
          tmp <- inla.mesh.project(proj.predref, result.predref$summary.random$spatial[,
                                                                                       "mean"])
          gf.quant.predref <- array(dim = c(nrow(tmp),
                                            ncol(tmp), n.quant))
          gf.quant.predref[, , 1] <- mean.quant[iquant] +
            tmp
        }
        else {
          gf.quant.predref[, , iquant] <- (mean.quant[iquant] +
                                             inla.mesh.project(proj.predref, result.predref$summary.random$spatial[,
                                                                                                                   "mean"]))
        }
      }
    }
    final.res <- append(final.res, list(mesh.predref = mesh.predref,
                                        proj.predref = proj.predref, u = u, v = v, cpu.used.predfreq.perloc = cpu.used.predfreq.perloc))
    if (use.geno) {
      final.res <- append(final.res, list(freq.predref = freq.predref))
    }
    if (use.quant) {
      final.res <- append(final.res, list(gf.quant.predref = gf.quant.predref,
                                          mean.quant = mean.quant, sd.noise.quant = sd.noise.quant))
    }
  }
  if (make.assign) {
    print("")
    print(" Assigning individuals of unknown origin")
    node.opt <- matrix(nrow = n.unknown, ncol = 2)
    ll <- array(dim = c(nrow(freq.predref[, , 1]), ncol(freq.predref[,
                                                                     , 1]), n.unknown), data = 0)
    for (iindiv in 1:n.unknown) {
      print(paste("indiv ", iindiv))
      if (use.geno) {
        for (iloc in 1:n.loc) {
          gg <- geno.unknown[iindiv, iloc]
          if (!is.na <http://is.na>(gg)) {
            ll[, , iindiv] <- ll[, , iindiv] + dbinom(x = gg,
                                                      size = ploidy, prob = as.vector(freq.predref[,
                                                                                                   , iloc]), log = TRUE)
          }
        }
      }
      if (use.quant) {
        for (iquant in 1:n.quant) {
          qq <- quant.unknown[iindiv, iquant]
          if (marginal.quant == "norm") {
            if (!is.na <http://is.na>(q)) {
              ll[, , iindiv] <- ll[, , iindiv] + dnorm(x = qq,
                                                       mean = gf.quant.predref[, , iquant],
                                                       sd = sd.noise.quant[iquant], log = TRUE)
            }
          }
          if (marginal.quant == "lnorm") {
            if (!is.na <http://is.na>(q)) {
              ll[, , iindiv] <- ll[, , iindiv] + dlnorm(x = qq,
                                                        meanlog = gf.quant.predref[, , iquant],
                                                        sdlog = sd.noise.quant[iquant], log = TRUE)
            }
          }
        }
      }
      mm <- max(ll[, , iindiv])
      node.opt[iindiv, ] <- which(ll[, , iindiv] == mm,
                                  arr.ind = TRUE)[1, ]
    }
    coord.unknown.est <- cbind(proj.predref$x[node.opt[,
                                                       1]], proj.predref$y[node.opt[, 2]])
    final.res <- append(final.res, list(ll = ll, coord.unknown.est = coord.unknown.est))
  }
  return(final.res)
}

#run analysis

res <- SPASIBA.test02(geno.ref=my_geno.ref,
                      ploidy=2,
                      coord.ref=my_coord.ref,
                      sphere=FALSE,
                      size.pop.ref=my_size.pop.ref,
                      geno.unknown=my_geno.unknown,
                      make.inf=TRUE,
                      loc.infcov = 1:30,
                      make.pred=TRUE,
                      make.assign=TRUE)

messages.body_plain:
Thank you for the advice. I’m not sure how to set beta.1 to 1 if it’s season 1 and NA if it’s season 2 in INLA.

I am considering defining u = f(x), then using f(e.season1, copy="u") + f(e.season2, copy="u"). Here, e.season1 is 1 when it’s season 1 and NA when it’s season 2, and the opposite for e.season2.

I’m not sure if this approach will achieve my goal, and I’m hesitant to add a linear predictor on u, as it might significantly increase computation time.

Thanks,
Rujia

>

messages.subject: Significance Spatial Effect
messages.body_plain:
Dear INLA community

I have been reading about how to fit multivariate spatial models and I found this paper

  Bayesian Inference for Multivariate Spatial Models with R-INLA by Francisco Palmí-Perales, Virgilio Gómez-Rubio, Roger S. Bivand, Michela Cameletti and Håvard Rue

Reading that I ended with some questions about the spatial modeling in a multivariate case

1-. If I want to check the significance of a shared spatial effect how can I do this without ignoring their correlation, I saw some examples using the DIC to check which model was the best (no spatial effect, one spatial effect, one shared spatial effect, or the individual and shared spatial effect) but I am not sure if there is any way to see the significance not just check how much does it changes

2-. In the paper I mentioned, at some point they plot the posterior of the shared spatial effect, the spatial effect for the first response, the spatial effect for the second response, and the specific effect of the second response, I am not sure what is the difference between the spatial effect of the second response, and the spatial specific effect of the second response. I add some image to explain myself better

3-. Reading the equations on that same paper they are defined like this

So my question is after following a bivariate model in INLA similar to the one you did, I want to use inla.posterior.sample.eval() to obtain samples from the posterior distribution for both of the responses it should be something like this

prediction_first <- function(){
     intercept.first + spatial_effect_first_response

}

prediction_second <- function(){
     intercept.second  + spatial_effect_shared + spatial_effect_second_response
}

In this case that spatial_effect_shared is created as a copy of the spatial_effect_first_response.

Is this correct?

Thank you for the help

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Significance Spatial Effect
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
To address questions of “significance” in correlated spatial field, you may want to consider the “excursions” package at https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/excursions/index.html and the papers linked there; it supports calculating joint level excursion sets for inla results. This is a “proper” way to address such “significance” questions that takes the correlation into account.
Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Mixed effect models in INLA
messages.body_plain:
The variable 'type' is categorical and its levels 'correct' the intercept. However, if these values are large then the priors on these regression parameter in INLA may cause the difference between INLA and glmer (I've seen that happening recently). Hence, my question is: Can you show the output from summary(mod.freq)

In normal words...if the mean values of your response variable differ substantially per `type` level, then the default values of the priors may be the reason that INLA and glmer results differ.

Alain

Thank you Dr Finn for your answer, I appreciate it.

Reading the package and the papers it mentions I have one doubt about how you address the spatial significance in one of them.
In "Calculating Probabilistic Excursion Sets and Related Quantities Using Excursions" I have some questions

1-. I see that you use tricontourmap in the case of spatial data. But I am not sure if I understood completely what is the interpretation of this, it is mentioned this

"We now want to find areas that likely experienced large amounts of precipitation. In the following code, we compute the excursion set for the posterior mean for the level 7 mm of precipitation."

The left is how excursion created the contours with the posterior mean to allow to see which places have a significant different mean on the response across the region.
Meanwhile the right shows the places with a significant spatial shared effect across the mesh?

Is that right? Also I see how the image in the right defines three regions but the left only has two, can that be attributed to the spatial effect?

Also following that idea of a bivariate model I would like to ask two questions:

1-. I would like to know if you have any paper where you use the posterior predictive distribution of a bivariate or multivariate model with inla.posterior.sample and inla.posterior.sample.eval?

2-. I am interested in obtaining the correlation between the sampled values of the two responses across the mesh, but right now I am obtaining a really low correlation so I would like to know if there is any reason for this (like the priors on the SPDE) or if that is just the nature of the samples obtained from the posterior predictive distributuion and not any prior that can be used in INLA would help to change that?

Thank you

My goal was to estimate the variance between schools within subcounties and between subcounties, by varying the random intercept, so, should the precision in the iid model be fixed or random? When I put the precision as fixed, I get the following output;

```

formula <- n ~ 1 +
  type +

  f(subcounty, model = "iid", hyper = list(prec = list(intial = -4, fixed = T))) +
  f(school_id, model = "iid", hyper = list(prec = list(intial = -4, fixed = T)))

> mod.inla  <- inla(
+   formula = formula,
+   family = 'binomial',
+   control.predictor=list(link = 1),
+   Ntrials = N,
+   data = df
+ )
>
> summary(mod.inla)
Time used:
    Pre = 1.58, Running = 0.589, Post = 0.0239, Total = 2.19
Fixed effects:
                       mean    sd 0.025quant 0.5quant 0.975quant   mode kld

 is computed
Posterior summaries for the linear predictor and the fitted values are computed
(Posterior marginals needs also 'control.compute=list(return.marginals.predictor=TRUE)')
```
The output does not contain the within and between variances/standard deviation.

2. In glmer, if the lower-level factor variable is uniquely labeled (for my case school_id), we know that specifying (1 | x/y) is equivalent to (1 | x) + (1 | y). When applying this concept in INLA, if I use the formula f(x, model = "iid") + f(y, model = "iid"), can I accurately describe this as having used nesting in the model?

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Significance Spatial Effect
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I think the left figure is showing the split into "clearly above" (blue), "clearly below" (light green), and "neither" (cyan).
In the right figure, the ark green areas show the join probabilities of being above; the precise definition is in the paper; it's a kind of "joint version" of the pontwise marginal exceedance probabilities; the dark blue excursion uncertainty set in the left figure I believe is an excursion set of those joint probabilities; "with probability xxx, this entire region is above the level".

I'm not sure if there's a paper that uses posterior samples (e.g. with excursions.mc <http://excursions.mc> that takes samples as input).

Not sure about your correlation question; it depends on the details of the model, and what the interpretation of the components is.

Finn

messages.subject: Random effects not behaving as expected
messages.subject_clean: Random effects not behaving as expected
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I hope you are well.

I am trying to run the following model to model dengue, but I am not getting the desired random effect for temperature, which should look like an inverted U.

Please see formula_1 below for the formula. I have count data, weekly (week_index) and by district(polyid). Temperature is mean temperature for each week for each district. As I was getting errors that the temperature data are too close to each other, I have rounded them. The offset is the log population of each district. The week effect is replicated at the province level (one admin level higher than district).

I first ran the model with diagonal = 1000 to get starting values, as was suggested in previous posts. In this model, the output looks somewhat like an inverted U shape. When I then re-ran the model using the first model as starting values, the output looks completely wrong – with a somewhat of a linear relationship with a sudden increase at higher temperatures. I have included the inla calls below.

I am not sure what might be wrong or how to proceed from here.

Any advice is much appreciated.

Many thanks,

Yalda

#priors

hyper.ar1 = list(theta1 = list(prior='pc.prec', param=c(0.5, 0.01)),

                 rho = list(prior='pc.cor0', param = c(0.5, 0.5)))

hyper3.rw <http://hyper3.rw> = list(prec = list(prior='pc.prec', param=c(1, 0.01)))

 hyper.bym2 = list(theta1 = list(prior="pc.prec", param=c(0.1, 0.01)),

                  theta2 = list(prior="pc", param=c(0.5, 0.5)))

#formula

formula_1 <-  count ~ 1 +

  offset(logpop) +

    f(week_index, model='ar1', hyper=hyper.ar1, constr=FALSE, replicate=provx) +

  f(round(temp, 1), model='rw2', hyper= hyper3.rw <http://hyper3.rw> , constr=T, scale.model = T) +

  f(polyid, model='bym2', graph=g,  scale.model=TRUE, adjust.for.con.comp=TRUE, hyper=hyper.bym2)

starting.value <- INLA::inla(

  formula_1,

  data,

  family = "zeroinflatedpoisson1",

  # fixed effects calibration

  control.fixed = list(mean.intercept=0,

                       prec.intercept=1,

                       mean=0,

                       prec=1),

  # save predicted values on response scale

  control.predictor = list(compute=TRUE,

                           link=1),

  # items to compute

  control.compute = list(cpo=TRUE,

                         waic=TRUE,

                         dic=TRUE,

                         config=TRUE,

                         return.marginals.predictor=TRUE ),

  # configure inla approx

  control.inla = list(int.strategy = 'eb',

                      strategy='gaussian',

                      cmin=0,

  diagonal = 1000),

   inla.mode = "experimental",

  verbose = TRUE

)

inla_result <- INLA::inla(

  formula_1,

  data,

  family = "zeroinflatedpoisson1",

  # fixed effects calibration

  control.fixed = list(mean.intercept=0,

                       prec.intercept=1,

                       mean=0,

                       prec=1),

  # save predicted values on response scale

  control.predictor = list(compute=TRUE,

                           link=1),

  # items to compute

  control.compute = list(cpo=TRUE,

                         waic=TRUE,

                         dic=TRUE,

                         config=TRUE,

                         return.marginals.predictor=TRUE ),

  # configure inla approx

  control.inla = list(int.strategy = 'eb',

                      strategy='adaptive' ,

                      cmin=0),

  control.mode = list(result = starting.value, restart = TRUE),

  inla.mode = "experimental",

  verbose = TRUE

)

messages.subject: Residual spatial fields
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am working on a model in inlabru with count data sampled on 9
different occasions. I'd like to demonstrate a general spatial pattern
in the data using a spatial field. But I'd also like to account for variation in the spatial
field across sampling occasions. So I am considering having two
spatial field terms in my model statement, one for a 'temporally
averaged' spatial field and one grouped version for the 'residuals'
around the temporally averaged term (see below). I suppose I could
just do a single grouped field, but I am hoping that the way I am
formulating the model below will make it easier to get predictions
for the average field. Does this approach make sense?

cmp1 <- count ~
    # global intercept
    Intercept(1) +
    # 'average' zero-centered spatial field?
     field(geometry, model = spde1) +
    # 'residual' zero-centered spatial fields?
     field_residuals(geometry, model = spde2, group = date_int,
                  control.group = list(model = 'iid', hyper = pc_prior))

# given
spde1 <- spde2 <- inla.spde2.pcmatern(
  mesh = mesh1,
  prior.range = c(10000, 0.5),
  prior.sigma = c(1, 0.01)
)

pc_prior <- list(prec = list(prior = "pc.prec", param = c(1, 0.01)))

predict(object=fit1, newdata=pix1, formula=exp(Intercept + field))

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Residual spatial fields
messages.body_plain:
Hi Rim,

Yes, in principle this makes sense. You just need to look out for potential nonidentifiability (the common field is confounded with the average of the residual fields). With 9 time points, this is probably ok, but you should check if the average of the residual fields has a noticeable spatial pattern. If it does, you might want to include that average pattern in the interpretation of the posterior common pattern.
Finn

messages.subject: sampling from the posterior of a fitted student-t regression model
messages.subject_clean: sampling from the posterior of a fitted student-t regression model
messages.body_plain:
If I have a model fitted with the Student t-family response, and want to draw samples of the response from the fitted model, is this the correct way to do, specifically for how the t response is parametrised in inla.doc("T"):

t_pp_draw <- function(inla_model, num_simulations) {
  # generate samples from the posterior
  samples <- inla.posterior.sample(n = num_simulations, result = inla_model)

  nu_loc <- grep("degrees of freedom for student-t", names(samples[[1]]$hyperpar))
  tau_loc <- grep("precision for the student-t observations", names(samples[[1]]$hyperpar))

  # the linear predictor
  eta <- inla.posterior.sample.eval("Predictor", samples)

  # the degrees of freedom for the student t
  nu <- inla.hyperpar.sample(n = num_simulations, result = inla_model)[, nu_loc]

  # the precision parameter
  tau <- inla.hyperpar.sample(n = num_simulations, result = inla_model)[, tau_loc]

  yvals <- matrix(NA, nrow = nrow(eta), ncol = num_simulations)
  for (i in 1:num_simulations) {
    yvals[, i] <- as.numeric(eta[, i]) + (rt(nrow(eta), df = nu[i]) / sqrt(tau[i]))
  }
  return(yvals)
}

Code largely adapted from how inlatools::distribution_check() is styled

Thanks.

messages.subject_clean: INLAjoint - sharing a frailty with longitudinal mixed model
messages.body_plain:
I am checking whether it is possible to share a frailty term in a recurrent events model with a linear mixed model (which includes a random intercept) using INLAjoint? i.e.

h_ik(t) = h_0(t) exp(B_0 + B_1 x_i + u_i)
y_ij(t) = A_0 + A_1 t_ij + A_2 x_i + gamma u_i + v_i

where x_i is a baseline binary covariate, u_i is a frailty and v_i a random intercept.

I have read what I can find about the "SRE" and "SRE_ind" association options but am still unsure - any insights gratefully received.

Many thanks, Keith
